16jun1529.summary: Jean du Bellay, bishop of Bayonne, to Montmorency from London, 16 June 1529: the clear text is about the bishopric he hoped for and a move against him; the cipher block advises, if his earlier counsel is followed (to pretend that Madame had not gone to conclude, and that Margaret of Austria, being there, had by importunity had a power sent for), to have that power dated from that time and from the place where the King will be (the Cambrai peace negotiation). Deciphered here from the leaf; Scheurer (1969) prints the same text.
16jun1529.en:
Monsieur, if you approve the advice I sent you some time ago — to pretend that Madame [Louise of Savoy] had not gone in
order to conclude, and that once she was there Madame Marguerite had, by importunity, made her send for powers — you must
not forget to have them dated from that time and from the place where the King [will] be.

22jun1529.summary: Du Bellay to Montmorency from London, 22 June 1529, with the Court decipherer's word-by-word interlinear reading on the leaf; printed by Le Grand, Histoire du divorce III (1688) pp. 327-332, and used here to re-derive the key.
22jun1529.en:
Letter of Monsieur du Bellay, Bishop of Bayonne, to Monsieur the Grand Maître.

Monseigneur, what has given them the hottest alarm is that the Duke of Suffolk has written to the King his master — I
have seen his very letter — that the King had told him that, when the Ladies came to this parley, everything would be
done and concluded in two days; on that they judge that matters are already agreed, that nothing is needed but a little
ceremony, saying that in this you have dealt too falsely with them, always showing them, saying and writing that you saw
no foundation in the matter. I assure you, Monseigneur, that without pretence the Lord Legate is in terrible distress,
for until this very hour he had always assured his master and everyone, in private and in public, that it would come to
nothing, and that you would do nothing whatever without them. He now strongly suspects the contrary;

17oct1529.summary: Du Bellay to Montmorency from London, 17 Oct 1529, on Wolsey's fall ("j'ay esté voir le Cardinal en ses ennuis"); printed by Le Grand III pp. 369-375 from a deciphered copy (Clair. 330 f. 71); the first cipher lines were deciphered here on the leaf as a check of the key.
17oct1529.en:
Letter of Monsieur du Bellay, Bishop of Bayonne, to Monsieur the Grand Maître.

Monseigneur, since the letters I thought to send at once, this despatch has been delayed until now, because the letters
I am sending you had to be made and remade a great many times, and for that reason there was much going and coming to
Windsor, both of the Dukes themselves and of others of this Council; and only now have they sent them to me in the form you
will see from the copy of them. They beg me as hard as they can to see that no one takes it ill if in these despatches,
and especially in what touches the main point of the despatch, I am not altogether satisfied as I would wish, nor they
themselves, excusing themselves that their way of negotiating with their master is not yet well settled;

30jun1529.summary: Du Bellay to Montmorency from London, last day of June 1529, about two of its four pages in cipher; printed in clear by Le Grand III pp. 333 ff. and calendared in L&P IV 5742; Tomokiyo's Clair. 329 f. 139 is the deciphered copy.
30jun1529.en:
Monseigneur, you will see from the King's letters part of what I could tell you of late, except to assure you that if the
Duke of Suffolk had a face of marble, the King had one of alabaster, seeing that you meant to press on; but that was not
without words. Nevertheless I forgive him, in my opinion, for he is somewhat timorous, and not only fears but is dying of
fear that, if the Emperor comes into Italy, the Pope will revoke his commission; whoever said I had done the work, when I
am with him, would be very much inclined to lie. I shall leave this talk; it would serve for nothing at present. I can
indeed tell you that when he does nothing of what you would wish, it will not be the fault of the Cardinal, who is wiser
than he, nor of any servant he has. Consider a little how he leads his people for you:

22oct1529.summary: Du Bellay to Montmorency from London, 22 Oct 1529: the ciphered opening, on granting the cardinal of York's request made through his Italian servant (Agostino, Wolsey's physician), had no known decipherment for Le Grand 1688, Brewer and Tomokiyo, but its decipherment is printed by Scheurer (1969); the clear part, on the Legate being turned out of his house, is in Le Grand III pp. 377-379.

system: 'Bayonne's cipher' of 1529: homophonic symbol alphabet with 2-5 signs per letter, a few nulls and word signs (roy, madame, bien, fault, paix, le Cardinal).
